Impression: Cerebellar vermian hypoplasia (Dandy-Walker variant) at 22 weeks gestation. The supratentorial brain is completely normal.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates a bicuspid aortic valve with fusion of the right and left coronary cusps. There is mild aortic stenosis with a peak velocity of 2.6 m/s across the valve. The ascending aorta is mildly dilated measuring 2.4 cm (Z-score +2.5). Left ventricular dimensions and systolic function are normal (LVEF 60%).

Impression: Bicuspid aortic valve with mild stenosis and mild dilation of the ascending aorta, requiring serial echocardiographic tracking.

High-resolution MR of the brain was performed to evaluate global developmental delay. Myelination pattern is appropriate for a 14-month-old infant. The ventricular system, extra-axial spaces, and major gray and white matter structures are normally formed. No areas of restricted diffusion, parenchymal hemorrhage, or pathological enhancement are visualized.

Impression: Normal pediatric brain MRI. No structural brain abnormalities or myelination delays are identified to account for the patient's developmental delay.

Brain MRI reveals multiple discrete, ovoid, hyperintense lesions on T2 and FLAIR sequences within the periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial white matter. Several lesions are oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles, resembling Dawson's fingers. Post-contrast imaging demonstrates active enhancement of two periventricular lesions, indicating active demyelination.

Impression: Findings are indicative of a demyelinating process, meeting the McDonald criteria for dissemination in space and time. Clinical correlation for pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis is advised.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 29 weeks gestation. The corpus callosum is partially formed, with the rostrum and anterior body present, but there is complete absence of the posterior body and splenium. There is mild elevation of the third ventricle and mild colpocephaly of the lateral ventricles, with the posterior atria measuring 9.5 mm on the left and 9.1 mm on the right. Sulcation pattern is appropriate.

Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated mild colpocephaly.

MRI of the brain demonstrates a well-demarcated cystic lesion within the left cerebellar hemisphere measuring 2.8 x 2.5 x 2.4 cm, containing a strongly enhancing mural nodule measuring 1.1 cm. There is mild localized mass effect on the fourth ventricle, but the basal cisterns remain patent and there is no evidence of supratentorial ventricular dilation. No abnormal parenchymal enhancement is seen elsewhere.

Impression: Findings are highly characteristic of a juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma. No acute obstructive hydrocephalus is present at this time.

MRI of the infant brain demonstrates severe, symmetrical dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles, with relative sparing of the fourth ventricle. There is severe narrowing and abrupt termination of the cerebral aqueduct. Thinning of the corpus callosum and flattening of the cortical gyri against the inner table of the skull are noted, along with mild periventricular FLAIR hyperintensity indicative of transependymal edema.

Impression: Severe obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to congenital aqueductal stenosis. There is active ventriculomegaly with transependymal cerebrospinal fluid migration, indicating the need for prompt neurosurgical intervention (e.g., third ventriculostomy or shunt placement).

Patient with history of d-Transposition of the Great Arteries (d-TGA) post-arterial switch operation. CMR shows normal neo-aortic root and neo-pulmonary root diameters. There is mild, asymptomatic supravalvular pulmonary stenosis at the anastomotic site, with a peak systolic gradient of 20 mmHg. Biventricular volume and global systolic function are completely normal (LVEF 62%, RVEF 55%). No coronary artery narrowing or myocardial perfusion defects are identified.

Impression: Status post arterial switch operation for d-TGA. Mild, hemodynamically insignificant supravalvular pulmonary stenosis with preserved biventricular volumes and function.

MR imaging of the brain demonstrates a solid, lobulated mass centered within the fourth ventricle, measuring 3.2 x 2.8 x 3.0 cm. The lesion is primarily T1-hypointense and T2-isointense, demonstrating restricted diffusion and heterogeneous contrast enhancement. The tumor causes complete obstruction of the fourth ventricle, resulting in severe non-communicating hydrocephalus with marked dilation of the lateral and third ventricles.

Impression: Fourth ventricular pediatric brain mass, most consistent with medulloblastoma, although ependymoma remains in the differential. Significant mass effect and secondary obstructive hydrocephalus are noted.

Fetal MRI at 23 weeks gestation demonstrates an open neural tube defect in the lumbar spine. There is a prominent defect in the posterior elements of the L3-L5 vertebrae, with herniation of meninges and neural placode. Secondary features of Chiari II malformation are evident, including a small posterior fossa, cerebellar vermian herniation (banana sign), and mild frontal bone scalloping (lemon sign). Bilateral ventricular atrial widths measure 12.5 mm, demonstrating moderate ventriculomegaly. Brain sulcal development is normal for 23 weeks.

Impression: Open lumbar myelomeningocele with associated Chiari II malformation and moderate bilateral ventriculomegaly.

Brain MRI was obtained for the diagnostic workup of cyclic vomiting syndrome and atypical migraines. Multisequence imaging demonstrates completely normal intracranial structure, with symmetric ventricles and sulci. No posterior fossa lesions, meningeal enhancement, or hydrocephalus are visualized.

Impression: Normal brain MRI. No structural abnormality, intracranial mass, or CSF obstruction to account for cyclic vomiting symptoms.

Cardiac MRI of a 13-year-old male demonstrates severe global dilation of the left ventricle with an end-diastolic volume index of 148 mL/m2. Left ventricular systolic function is severely depressed with an ejection fraction of 31%. Diffuse, mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement is noted within the septum, consistent with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. Right ventricular size and function are at the lower limit of normal (RVEF 48%).

Impression: Severe dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with globally depressed left ventricular systolic function and septal fibrosis.

MRI of the brain shows a large, cystic lesion within the right cerebellar hemisphere, measuring 3.5 x 3.2 cm, containing a strongly enhancing mural nodule measuring 1.2 cm. There is associated mass effect compressing the fourth ventricle and leading to moderate upstream dilation of the lateral and third ventricles. Surrounding vasogenic edema is minimal, and no supratentorial abnormalities are seen.

Impression: Cystic cerebellar lesion with an enhancing mural nodule, highly characteristic of a juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma. Secondary obstructive hydrocephalus is present.

Fetal MRI at 33 weeks gestation demonstrates a large sacrococcygeal teratoma (SCT). There is a large, lobulated, mixed cystic and solid mass arising from the sacrococcygeal region, extending externally and pelvic-ward. It measures approximately 7.5 x 6.2 cm. High vascularity and mild cardiomegaly are noted, indicating a high-output fetal cardiac state. Fetal brain imaging shows normal sulcation for 33 weeks, and the lateral ventricular atrium is normal at 5.6 mm.

Impression: Large, predominantly external (Type I) sacrococcygeal teratoma with signs of mild fetal cardiac volume overload.

The study was designed to evaluate an anomalous coronary artery origin in a 15-year-old female presenting with exertional syncope. MR angiography reveals that the left main coronary artery (LMCA) originates anomalously from the right coronary sinus. Importantly, the LMCA takes an interarterial course between the aorta and the main pulmonary artery, demonstrating slit-like ostial narrowing and significant acute-angled takeoff.

Impression: Anomalous origin of the left main coronary artery from the right sinus of Valsalva with a high-risk interarterial course. This finding is associated with an elevated risk of myocardial ischemia and sudden cardiac death during exertion.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation reveals symmetric and unremarkable cerebral hemispheres. Sulcation and migration are progressing normally for this gestational age. The lateral ventricles are completely normal, with the atrium measuring 5.8 mm on the left and 5.6 mm on the right. The midline structures, including the corpus callosum and cavum septum pellucidum, are clearly visualized and morphologically intact.

The posterior fossa, spine, and all thoracic and abdominal structures are unremarkable. Impression: Unremarkable fetal MRI demonstrating completely normal 24-week development of the brain, spine, and major organs.

Cardiac MRI evaluates for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). The right ventricle is dilated and shows regional wall motion abnormalities, specifically dyskinesis and microaneurysm formation in the RV outflow tract and inferior wall. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging shows extensive subepicardial and mid-myocardial fibrosis involving the right ventricular free wall, extending into the basal septum of the left ventricle.

Impression: Features highly suggestive of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting multiple task force criteria including RV dilation, regional dyskinesis, and characteristic fibrous infiltration. Left ventricular ejection fraction is mildly reduced at 50%.

CMR demonstrates both the aorta and the pulmonary artery arising almost entirely from the right ventricle. There is a large subaortic ventricular septal defect (VSD) measuring approximately 8 mm, allowing for partial communication with the left ventricle. Right ventricular hypertrophy is present. The left ventricle is relatively small but demonstrates normal contractility (LVEF 55%). No pulmonary stenosis is identified on the current study.

Impression: Double Outlet Right Ventricle (DORV) with a large subaortic VSD. No evidence of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

Cardiac MR imaging demonstrates a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, which measures up to 14 mm in posterior thickness and 10 mm anteriorly. There is no evidence of diastolic collapse of the right atrium or right ventricle, and respiratory septal bounce is absent, suggesting no immediate tamponade physiology. Biventricular dimensions and systolic function are preserved (LVEF 60%, RVEF 56%) with no signs of myocardial edema.

Impression: Moderate circumferential pericardial effusion without evidence of hemodynamic compromise or cardiac tamponade. No associated myocardial involvement or active myocarditis is appreciated.

Brain MRI was performed to evaluate developmental delay. The myelination of white matter structures is symmetric and corresponds normally to a child of 2 years of age. Ventricles, sulci, and extra-axial spaces are normal in size. There is no evidence of intracranial mass, structural malformation, or focal signal abnormalities.

Impression: Normal pediatric brain MRI demonstrating age-appropriate myelination and no structural or metabolic anomalies.

MR evaluation of the brain reveals a well-defined cystic mass with an eccentrically located, strongly enhancing mural nodule in the left cerebellar hemisphere. The lesion measures approximately 2.8 x 2.4 x 2.5 cm and exerts moderate mass effect on the fourth ventricle, causing partial compression and mild upstream dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles. Surrounding vasogenic edema is minimal, and myelination pattern corresponds to normal standards for an 11-month-old infant.

Impression: Cystic cerebellar lesion with an enhancing mural nodule, highly characteristic of a juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma. Mild secondary obstructive hydrocephalus is noted.

MR imaging shows significant thickening and elevated T2/FLAIR signal of the intraorbital and canalicular segments of the left optic nerve. Mild enhancement is noted along the visual pathway, extending post-chiasmatically. The contralateral optic nerve appears structurally normal, and there are no other focal intracranial abnormalities.

Impression: Left optic pathway glioma. Given the presentation, clinical correlation and genetic screening for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is highly recommended.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation demonstrates a large, multicystic left kidney containing multiple non-communicating cysts of varying sizes up to 1.8 cm, with no normal surrounding parenchyma visible. The right kidney is normal in size and signal intensity, and the bladder is filled, indicating preserved overall renal function. Intracranial anatomy is completely normal with a ventricular atrial width of 5.9 mm and normal 26-week sulcation.

Amniotic fluid volume is normal. Impression: Left multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) with a normal, hypertrophied right kidney and normal amniotic fluid volume, suggesting adequate total renal function.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates significant, symmetric dilation of the lateral ventricles. The left and right ventricular atria measure 14.8 mm and 15.2 mm, respectively, indicating severe bilateral ventriculomegaly. There is corresponding thinning of the periventricular white matter, but the cortical sulcation pattern is otherwise normal and appropriate for 28 weeks. The corpus callosum is present and intact, and no intracranial hemorrhage or destructive parenchymal lesions are identified.

The remaining fetal anatomy, including the posterior fossa and spinal column, appears unremarkable. Impression: Severe bilateral fetal ventriculomegaly. Close clinical surveillance and postnatal neurosurgical evaluation are recommended.

MR imaging of the brain was performed using multiplanar, multisequence protocols. The brain parenchyma is normal in signal intensity and morphology without evidence of focal mass, acute ischemia, or intracranial hemorrhage. The ventricular system, basal cisterns, and major sulci are normal in size and configuration for the patient's age. The major intracranial arterial flow voids are preserved.

Visualized paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells are well-aerated. Impression: Normal pediatric brain MRI. No structural abnormality, vascular pathology, or acute findings identified to explain the clinical presentation of chronic headaches.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates normal growth and structural anatomy. The lateral ventricles are completely symmetric, with the left and right atria measuring 6.5 mm. The opercular and insular sulcation is symmetric and entirely appropriate for 29 weeks. The posterior fossa structures, corpus callosum, and fetal abdominal and thoracic organs show normal development.

Impression: Normal fetal MRI study at 29 weeks gestation. Symmetric, age-appropriate intracranial development and ventricular measurements.

Cardiac MRI performed for evaluation of a dynamic, posture-dependent systolic murmur. Left and right ventricular end-diastolic volumes, myocardial mass, and wall thickness are within normal parameters. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 65% and right ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. The cardiac valves are thin, mobile, and normal in appearance. No intra- or extra-cardiac shunts are identified, and there is no late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Completely normal pediatric cardiac MRI. No congenital anomalies, shunts, or structural valve disease identified.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation demonstrates completely normal anatomy. The cerebral hemispheres are symmetric, exhibiting early development of the precentral and postcentral sulci, in line with expected maturation. The lateral ventricular atria measure 5.9 mm bilaterally. The interhemispheric structures, including the corpus callosum and cavum septum pellucidum, are clearly visualized and normal.

Fetal limbs, abdominal wall, and chest cavity are unremarkable. Impression: Normal fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation. No morphological anomalies identified.

Large secundum-type atrial septal defect (ASD) measuring 18 mm in maximum diameter. There is a substantial left-to-right shunt with a calculated Qp/Qs ratio of 1.9:1. Mild to moderate dilation of both the right atrium and right ventricle is present, reflecting a volume overload pattern. Left-sided chambers are normal in size with preserved systolic function.

Impression: Large secundum atrial septal defect with significant left-to-right shunt and resulting right-sided chamber volume overload. Right ventricular EF is normal at 60%.

Cardiac MRI was performed to evaluate for potential structural anomalies or cardiomyopathy in a 3-year-old female with an atypical murmur. Assessment of the cardiac chambers reveals normal bi-atrial and bi-ventricular volumes. The left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 62%, and the right ventricular ejection fraction is 58%, both well within normal pediatric parameters. There is no evidence of intracardiac shunt, valvular stenosis, or regurgitation, and the great vessels demonstrate normal branching patterns and calibers.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. No structural congenital heart disease, ventricular dysfunction, or pathologic late gadolinium enhancement is identified.

There is a ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe measuring 2.1 x 1.9 cm. The lesion demonstrates restricted central diffusion on DWI and is surrounded by a prominent zone of T2/FLAIR hyperintense vasogenic edema, producing mild compression of the left lateral ventricle frontal horn. Visualized paranasal sinuses show acute mucosal thickening.

Impression: Left frontal ring-enhancing lesion with extensive surrounding edema, highly concerning for a cerebral abscess, potentially secondary to paranasal sinusitis.

Cardiovascular MRI of a 20-year-old male with a history of tricuspid atresia post-Fontan palliation. There is a patent extra-cardiac Fontan conduit showing laminar flow without focal narrowing. The single left ventricle is dilated (EDVI 120 ml/m²) and demonstrates mild systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 46%.

No thrombi or focal stenoses are seen in the systemic venous pathway or pulmonary arteries. There is mild, diffuse late gadolinium enhancement within the single ventricular myocardium. Impression: Post-Fontan circulation for tricuspid atresia, with a patent conduit and mild single ventricular systolic dysfunction.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation demonstrates partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior aspect (genu and body) of the corpus callosum is present, but the posterior body and splenium are absent. The posterior horns of the lateral ventricles show mild colpocephalic dilation, measuring 10.8 mm. The cerebral sulcation and gyration are appropriate for 31 weeks gestation, and the posterior fossa structures are normal.

Impression: Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum involving the splenium and posterior body, with mild colpocephaly. No other brain anomalies are seen.

MRI of the brain, orbits, and posterior fossa demonstrates normal intracranial structures. The craniocervical junction is intact. No cerebellar tonsillar ectopia is seen. No focal lesions are noted in the fourth ventricle, brainstem, or hypothalamus, and no abnormal enhancement is demonstrated.

Impression: Normal MR imaging of the brain. No structural, inflammatory, or neoplastic changes identified in relation to the patient's symptoms of cyclical vomiting.

Fetal MRI at 30 weeks gestation shows bilateral, symmetric ventriculomegaly. The left lateral ventricular atrium measures 14.2 mm, and the right lateral ventricular atrium measures 13.8 mm, indicating moderate-to-severe ventriculomegaly. There is mild thinning of the overlying cerebral cortex, but the sulcation pattern remains appropriate for 30 weeks gestation. The corpus callosum and posterior fossa structures are fully present and normal.

No aqueductal stenosis, intraventricular hemorrhage, or other structural abnormalities are detected. Impression: Isolated moderate-to-severe bilateral fetal ventriculomegaly.

MR imaging of the brain demonstrates normal ventricular size, normal sulcation, and clear, symmetric subarachnoid spaces. The gray-white matter boundaries are well-demarcated, and there are no signs of intracranial hemorrhage, ischemia, mass effect, or pathological dural enhancement. No vascular anomalies are visualized on the screening 3D TOF sequences.

Impression: Unremarkable and completely normal brain MRI study. No underlying parenchymal, ventricular, or large vascular abnormalities seen.

Cardiac MRI of an 8-month-old infant demonstrates a moderately large perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) measuring 8 mm. Flow analysis demonstrates a significant left-to-right shunt with a Qp/Qs ratio of 1.8:1. There is mild dilation of both the left atrium and left ventricle, indicative of volume overload of the pulmonary venous receiving chambers. Left ventricular ejection fraction is normal at 62%.

Impression: Moderate-to-large perimembranous ventricular septal defect with a significant left-to-right shunt and early left-sided volume overload.

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks gestation demonstrates severe skeletal dysplasia. There is profound symmetric shortening of all long bones, including the femurs and humeri, which measure well below the 5th percentile for gestational age. The ribs are severely shortened and thin, resulting in a narrow, bell-shaped thoracic cavity with significant restriction of lung volume. There is associated macrocephaly and frontal bossing.

Intracranial anatomy is intact, with appropriate sulcation for 27 weeks. Lateral ventricular atria measure 7.1 mm. Impression: Severe skeletal dysplasia, highly suspicious for a lethal osteochondrodysplasia such as thanatophoric dysplasia, given the narrow thoracic cavity and severe micromelia.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation reveals an open neural tube defect in the lumbar spine, consistent with a myelomeningocele. This is accompanied by classic signs of a Chiari II malformation, including effacement of the posterior fossa CSF spaces, a crowded posterior fossa, herniation of the hindbrain, and a 'banana-shaped' cerebellum. Frontal bone scalloping (the 'lemon sign') is noted. The lateral ventricles are moderately dilated, with atria measuring 12.8 mm on the left and 12.5 mm on the right.

Impression: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele with associated Chiari II malformation and moderate ventriculomegaly. Fetal surgery evaluation and genetic counseling are recommended.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates a large, non-restrictive perimembranous ventricular septal defect (VSD) measuring approximately 8.5 mm in diameter. There is significant left-to-right shunting, calculated with a pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp/Qs) of 2.1:1. Moderate dilation of both the left atrium and left ventricle is present, reflecting significant volume overload. Left ventricular ejection fraction is maintained at 58%. The right ventricle is mildly hypertrophied but has normal systolic function (RVEF 55%).

Impression: Large perimembranous ventricular septal defect with a high-volume left-to-right shunt (Qp/Qs = 2.1) and secondary left-sided chamber enlargement, consistent with hemodynamically significant volume overload. Surgical closure is indicated.

Fetal MRI performed at 28 weeks gestation. There is prominent bilateral ventricular dilation, more pronounced on the left side where the atrium of the lateral ventricle measures 15.5 mm, indicating severe ventriculomegaly. The right lateral ventricular atrium measures 11.2 mm (moderate ventriculomegaly). The cerebral cortex demonstrates sulcation appropriate for 28 weeks, with expected progression of the parieto-occipital and calcarine fissures. The corpus callosum is present but appears globally thinned, likely secondary to passive compression from the dilated ventricles.

Impression: Severe left-sided and moderate right-sided fetal ventriculomegaly at 28 weeks gestation. Close follow-up with serial neurosonography is recommended to monitor ventricular dynamics, and pediatric neurosurgical consultation is suggested.

Cardiac MRI evaluates an 11-year-old male with persistent pericardial chest pain following a viral illness. Standard cine imaging reveals a moderate-to-large, free-flowing, circumferential pericardial effusion measuring up to 18 mm in the posterolateral pericardial space. No diastolic collapse of the right atrium or right ventricle is seen to suggest tamponade physiology. The pericardium itself is thickened and demonstrates intense late enhancement, indicative of active pericardial inflammation. Global bi-ventricular size and function are preserved, with an LVEF of 55%.

Impression: Moderate-to-large circumferential pericardial effusion with active, severe pericarditis. No physiological findings of cardiac tamponade on this supine scan.

MRI demonstrates a lobulated, complex suprasellar mass measuring 2.8 x 2.4 x 2.1 cm. The lesion contains cystic components and demonstrates peripherally calcified/hypointense areas on susceptibility imaging. Strong, heterogeneous cystic-wall enhancement is present following gadolinium administration. The mass compresses the optic chiasm and displaces the third ventricle superiorly, leading to mild lateral ventricular dilation.

Impression: Complex suprasellar cystic mass compressing the optic chiasm, characteristic of adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.

MRI study of the brain demonstrates normal anatomical structure. The cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem are structurally intact and show no signal abnormalities on T1, T2, or FLAIR sequences. There is no evidence of microhemorrhage, cytotoxic edema, or extra-axial fluid collections. The ventricular system, sulci, and basal cisterns are age-appropriate and unremarkable.

Impression: Normal MR of the brain with no evidence of acute traumatic injury, intracranial bleeding, or structural lesions in this adolescent with persistent post-concussive symptoms.

Cardiac MRI reveals signs of acute myocarditis. Multi-sequence imaging demonstrates patchy subepicardial and mid-myocardial edema on T2-weighted and T2-mapping sequences, primarily involving the lateral and inferior free walls of the left ventricle. Late gadolinium enhancement imaging confirms prominent patchy subepicardial enhancement in the corresponding areas. LVEF is mildly reduced at 48% with mild global hypokinesia.

Impression: Findings highly consistent with acute myocarditis based on Updated Lake Louise Criteria. Mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction is present.

Brain MRI shows a mixed cystic and solid suprasellar mass measuring 2.3 x 1.9 x 2.1 cm. The lesion is causing compression of the optic chiasm and elevating the floor of the third ventricle. The solid component demonstrates heterogeneous enhancement, and peripheral rim enhancement of the cystic portion is seen. No significant hydrocephalus is present.

Impression: Suprasellar mixed solid and cystic mass, highly characteristic of a pediatric adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma. Mass effect on the optic chiasm is observed.

MR angiogram and brain MRI reveal an abnormal nidus of dilated, tortuous vascular flow voids in the left parietal lobe measuring approximately 2.3 x 1.8 cm. The lesion is fed by branches of the left middle cerebral artery and drains into a dilated cortical vein which drains into the superior sagittal sinus. There is no surrounding edema, mass effect, or evidence of acute or chronic parenchymal hemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging.

Impression: Left parietal vascular malformation consistent with a non-ruptured arteriovenous malformation (AVM). Intervention planning via formal catheter cerebral angiography is recommended.

Brain MRI was obtained to investigate a history of atypical syncopal episodes. Multiplanar T1, T2, FLAIR, and DWI sequences reveal normal intracranial structures. The brainstem, cerebellum, and cerebral hemispheres are free of signal abnormalities. Cerebellar tonsils are normally positioned, and the main intracranial flow voids are intact.

Impression: Completely normal brain MRI. No structural abnormality or neurovascular disease identified to account for syncopal events.

MRI of the brain shows multiple subependymal nodules projecting into the lateral ventricles, with a larger, growing nodule at the left foramen of Monro measuring 1.2 cm, which demonstrates heterogeneous enhancement. Several cortical tubers are also identified in both cerebral hemispheres.

Impression: Features consistent with tuberous sclerosis complex, including subependymal nodules and cortical tubers. The enlarging lesion at the left foramen of Monro is highly suspicious for a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA).

MR study of the brain shows excellent differentiation of gray and white matter. The ventricles and extra-axial CSF spaces are within normal limits for age. No focal areas of restricted diffusion, parenchymal mass, or abnormal enhancement are observed. Internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles are clear.

Impression: Completely normal brain MRI. No evidence of a structural basis, intracranial mass, or vascular anomaly to explain chronic headache complaints.

MRI brain demonstrates multiple subependymal nodules projecting into the lateral ventricles, particularly clustered near the caudothalamic grooves. Several of these nodules demonstrate low T2 signal intensity, suggestive of calcification. There are also multiple cortical and subcortical FLAIR hyperintense lesions (cortical tubers) and radial migration lines within both cerebral hemispheres. No subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) is identified.

Impression: Brain MRI findings are diagnostic of tuberous sclerosis complex. No evidence of a transforming subependymal giant cell astrocytoma at the foramen of Monro.

Cine and structural cardiac MRI demonstrate normal myocardial thickness and normal ventricular volumes. The left ventricular ejection fraction is 65% and the right ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. There is no evidence of regional wall motion abnormality, myocardial edema on T2 sequences, or late gadolinium enhancement to suggest focal fibrosis. Valve leaflets are thin and mobile with trace physiological tricuspid regurgitation.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI with excellent biventricular function and no structural or tissue-level abnormalities.

Fetal MRI performed at 30 weeks gestation demonstrates borderline isolated bilateral ventriculomegaly. The left lateral ventricular atrium measures 10.2 mm, and the right atrium measures 10.4 mm. The septum pellucidum is present, and the corpus callosum is intact. Sulcation patterns show appropriate depth and complexity for 30 weeks, including well-defined superior temporal and central sulci.

No other structural brain lesions or extracranial anomalies are identified. Amniotic fluid is normal. Impression: Mild, borderline bilateral ventriculomegaly without associated intracranial or extracranial anomalies. Close follow-up is recommended.

The study demonstrates Ebstein's anomaly of the tricuspid valve, characterized by marked apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve (displacement index > 8 mm/m2). This results in prominent 'atrialization' of the inflow portion of the right ventricle. Severe tricuspid regurgitation is present, leading to massive dilatation of the right atrium and the atrialized right ventricle.

Impression: Classic Ebstein's anomaly with severe tricuspid regurgitation and massive right atrial dilatation. Right ventricular systolic function is mildly reduced (RVEF 47%).

Cardiac MRI shows normal ventricular size and systolic function (LVEF 62%, RVEF 58%). However, there is a moderate, circumferential pericardial effusion measuring up to 1.4 cm along the posterior and lateral left ventricular walls. There is no diastolic collapse of the right atrium or right ventricle to suggest cardiac tamponade. No abnormal pericardial thickening or delayed enhancement is noted.

Impression: Moderate circumferential pericardial effusion without current MRI criteria for hemodynamic tamponade. Myocardium demonstrates normal signal characteristics.

Sagittal and axial imaging of the brain demonstrates herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 8 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. There is mild effacement of the retrocerebellar cerebrospinal fluid spaces, though no syrinx is noted within the visualized cervical spinal cord. The supratentorial ventricular system and cortical sulcation are within normal limits for age, and there are no signs of intracranial pressure elevation.

Impression: Chiari I malformation with 8 mm cerebellar tonsillar herniation. No associated syringomyelia or obstructive hydrocephalus is identified on the current scan.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 22 weeks gestation reveals a normal fetus. The brain exhibits expected sulcation and migration patterns for 22 weeks, with visible sylvian fissures. The ventricles are normal in size, with both atria measuring 5.6 mm. The corpus callosum is intact, and the cerebellum is normal.

Chest and abdominal anatomy are unremarkable, and there is no evidence of fetal masses or diaphragmatic defects. Impression: Completely normal fetal MRI study demonstrating age-appropriate structural development at 22 weeks gestation.

Fetal MRI at 22 weeks gestation is performed to evaluate suspected renal pathology. There is a near-total absence of amniotic fluid (severe oligohydramnios), which limits image resolution. Both renal fossae are empty, and no renal tissue or renal arteries are identified. The fetal urinary bladder is non-distended and not visualized, confirming renal agenesis. The fetal chest is small, indicating early pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal brain structures are within normal limits despite oligohydramnios artifacts. Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis associated with severe oligohydramnios and early-stage pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal MRI at 34 weeks gestation demonstrates a right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. There is herniation of the right hepatic lobe, gallbladder, and portions of the small bowel into the right hemithorax, resulting in leftward displacement of the heart and mediastinum. The right lung is severely hypoplastic, and the left lung is compressed with an estimated total fetal lung volume significantly below expected values. The fetal brain shows normal cortical development and sulcation for 34 weeks.

Impression: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver-up herniation and severe pulmonary hypoplasia. This represents a high-risk case requiring delivery at a tertiary pediatric surgical facility.

Brain MRI of an 8-month-old infant demonstrates peg-like herniation of the cerebellar tonsils approximately 8 mm below the level of the foramen magnum. There is effacement of the cisterna magna and compression of the cervicomedullary junction. Significant dilation of the lateral and third ventricles is observed, accompanied by thinning and elevation of the corpus callosum.

Impression: Chiari I malformation with associated moderate supratentorial hydrocephalus. Urgent neurosurgical assessment is recommended for potential posterior fossa decompression.

Brain MRI demonstrates a complex, cystic and solid suprasellar mass measuring 3.1 x 2.8 cm. The lesion shows peripheral nodular calcification on gradient echo sequences and cystic areas with variable signal intensity. The optic chiasm is elevated and severely compressed. The mass exerts mass effect on the hypothalamus and pituitary stalk, with posterior displacement.

Impression: Suprasellar lesion, highly characteristic of a craniopharyngioma (adamantinomatous type given the age and cystic/calcified appearance). Endocrine and neuro-ophthalmic evaluations are recommended.

Brain MRI reveals a solid, hypercellular, midline mass in the posterior fossa arising from the roof of the fourth ventricle. The tumor is measuring 3.5 x 3.0 cm, showing restricted diffusion on DWI sequences and moderate heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast imaging. The fourth ventricle is compressed, causing severe obstructive hydrocephalus with transependymal CSF migration.

Impression: Midline cerebellar mass with associated obstructive hydrocephalus, most suggestive of a medulloblastoma. Spinal MRI is recommended to evaluate for drop metastases.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal systemic and pulmonary venous return. The right and left atria and ventricles are normal in size, and the myocardial mass is appropriate for the patient's body surface area. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 61% and right ventricular ejection fraction is 57%, with no regional wall motion abnormalities or areas of focal dyskinesia.

There is no evidence of intracardiac shunt, valvular stenosis, or regurgitation. Myocardial perfusion and late gadolinium enhancement sequences are normal. Impression: Normal pediatric cardiac MRI with preserved ventricular volumes and systolic function.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was obtained following a sports-related concussion. There is no evidence of intracranial hematoma, subdural or epidural fluid collections, or focal contusion. Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) demonstrates no microhemorrhages or axonal injury patterns. Ventricles and sulci are normal, and no pathological enhancement is identified.

Impression: Completely normal MR imaging of the brain. No structural correlate or post-traumatic changes identified to explain persistent post-concussion syndrome symptoms.

Cardiac MRI reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximum diastolic wall thickness of 22 mm at the anterior interventricular septum. There is systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve leaflet, resulting in moderate mitral regurgitation and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging shows patchy, mid-myocardial enhancement at the septal insertion points, indicative of focal myocardial fibrosis. Left ventricular ejection fraction is hyperdynamic at 75%.

Impression: Classic phenotypic features of asymmetric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with LVOT obstruction and associated patchy myocardial fibrosis.

Cardiac MRI shows a large secundum-type atrial septal defect (ASD) measuring 12 mm in maximum dimension. Phase-contrast velocity mapping demonstrates a significant left-to-right shunt with a Qp/Qs ratio of 1.8:1. There is notable dilation of the right atrium and right ventricle, reflecting chronic volume overload. The right ventricular end-diastolic volume index is elevated at 115 mL/m2. Right ventricular systolic function is preserved with an ejection fraction of 57%. Left-sided chambers are normal in size.

Impression: Large secundum atrial septal defect with significant right-sided chamber dilation and volume overload (Qp/Qs = 1.8). Discussion of elective closure options is recommended.

Cardiac MRI in a 19-year-old female with a history of ventricular tachycardia. The right ventricle is moderately dilated (RVEDVI 122 ml/m²) with areas of dyskinesia and micro-aneurysms noted in the right ventricular free wall and outflow tract. Myocardial tissue characterization demonstrates focal areas of fat infiltration and transmural late gadolinium enhancement within the right ventricular free wall, indicative of fibrofatty replacement. Right ventricular ejection fraction is depressed at 38%. The left ventricle is normal in size and function (LVEF 52%).

Impression: Morphological and tissue characterization features highly characteristic of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting major task force criteria.

Cardiac MRI of a 12-year-old male reveals prominent left ventricular trabeculation, particularly in the apex and lateral wall. The non-compacted to compacted myocardial ratio at end-diastole is 2.4. Left ventricular systolic function is mildly depressed with an ejection fraction of 48%.

Impression: Features highly characteristic of Left Ventricular Non-Compaction (LVNC) with mild global systolic dysfunction. No late gadolinium enhancement is noted.

High-resolution pediatric cardiac MRI demonstrates normal biventricular dimensions and systolic function. The calculated left ventricular ejection fraction is 64% and the right ventricular ejection fraction is 59%. There are no septal defects or extracardiac shunts, and the ventricular wall thickness is appropriate for the patient's age and body surface area. Myocardial tissue characterization via T1 and T2 mapping is entirely normal with no pathological late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. No evidence of congenital heart disease, focal fibrosis, or myocardial inflammation.

Cardiac MRI performed for screening of a 4-year-old female with a history of Kawasaki disease resolved two years prior. High-resolution MR angiography of the coronary arteries demonstrates normal anatomy. The main left coronary artery, left anterior descending, circumflex, and right coronary arteries are normal in course and caliber without evidence of dilation, ectasia, or aneurysm. Left and right ventricular chamber sizes, wall thicknesses, and global systolic function are completely normal (LVEF 62%, RVEF 59%).

Impression: Unremarkable cardiac MRI showing normal coronary artery anatomy and normal ventricular function. No sequelae of Kawasaki disease are identified.

Fetal MRI at 22 weeks gestation reveals a severe intracranial malformation. There is a single, large, monoventricle in the center of the brain cavity, with complete absence of the midline structures including the septum pellucidum and the interhemispheric fissure. The thalami are partially fused at the midline. Prominent facial dysmorphism is noted, including a cleft lip and palate and hypotelorism. The posterior fossa structures are normal, but cerebral parenchyma is thinned anteriorly.

Impression: Semilobar holoprosencephaly associated with midline facial clefting and hypotelorism. Given the severity of the malformations, urgent genetic counseling and pediatric multidisciplinary counseling are advised.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation evaluates renal anatomy. The left kidney is replaced by multiple, non-communicating cysts of varying sizes, the largest measuring 1.8 cm, with no normal-appearing renal parenchyma identified, consistent with a multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK). The right kidney is hypertrophied but otherwise normal in appearance, with preserved corticomedullary differentiation. Amniotic fluid volume is normal. The fetal brain shows normal anatomy with lateral ventricle atrial measurements of 5.9 mm.

Impression: Unilateral left multicystic dysplastic kidney. The contralateral right kidney appears healthy and compensatory, with normal amniotic fluid volume suggesting preserved overall renal function.

Brain MRI demonstrates multiple subependymal nodules lining the lateral ventricles, some of which demonstrate signal characteristics suggestive of calcification. Additionally, multiple hyperintense cortical and subcortical lesions (tubers) are seen on T2 and FLAIR sequences throughout the bilateral cerebral hemispheres. A prominent 1.1 cm enhancing nodule near the left foramen of Monro is visualized, showing no interval growth compared to prior exams but requiring close tracking.

Impression: Findings are classic for tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Stable subependymal nodule near the left foramen of Monro without signs of current obstruction.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation shows complete agenesis of the corpus callosum combined with moderate ventriculomegaly. The lateral ventricles display a parallel configuration and colpocephaly, with the atrium of the posterior horn measuring 13.1 mm. The third ventricle is superiorly displaced and dilated. Cortical sulcation is appropriate for 25 weeks, showing early Sylvian fissure and cingulate sulcus development.

No other midline or posterior fossa anomalies are identified. Impression: Agenesis of the corpus callosum with associated moderate bilateral ventriculomegaly.

Brain MRI performed as a routine follow-up after treatment for bacterial meningitis. There is no persistent leptomeningeal enhancement on post-contrast imaging. The ventricular size has returned to baseline with no signs of hydrocephalus. No focal areas of cerebral tissue loss or cerebritis are identified.

Impression: Normal brain MRI with complete resolution of prior meningitis features. No chronic sequelae or abnormal intracranial enhancement observed.

MR evaluation of the brain reveals normal cranial anatomy. The cerebral cortex, white matter, and deep gray nuclei are within normal limits for a 14-year-old. The ventricles and subarachnoid spaces are symmetric. No acute traumatic, structural, or vascular abnormalities are identified.

Impression: Completely normal brain MRI. No evidence of intracranial pathology, mass, or subacute hemorrhage.

Brain MR imaging in this 8-month-old infant demonstrates a generalized symmetric enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces, particularly within the frontal regions. The ventricles are normal to minimally prominent, with no thinning of the corpus callosum or evidence of CSF outflow obstruction. The cerebral parenchyma and myelination pattern are age-appropriate.

Impression: Benign macrocephaly of infancy (benign external hydrocephalus). This is a self-limiting developmental variant with no evidence of pathological intracranial hypertension.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal cardiac anatomy, chamber sizes, and ventricular function. The left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (LVEDVI) is 74 mL/m2, with a calculated ejection fraction of 62%. The right ventricle is normal in size and demonstrates preserved systolic function with an ejection fraction of 59%. There is no evidence of myocardial edema, perfusion defects, or late gadolinium enhancement (LGE).

Impression: Completely normal cardiac MRI study. No evidence of cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, or congenital structural anomalies.

Multiplanar MR imaging reveals a large, lobulated, hypercellular mass in the pineal region measuring approximately 2.9 x 2.7 cm. The lesion demonstrates intermediate signal on T2, restricted diffusion, and heterogeneous contrast enhancement with calcification/cystic areas. There is associated compression of the cerebral aqueduct, leading to moderate ventriculomegaly of the third and lateral ventricles.

Impression: Pineal region mass with secondary obstructive hydrocephalus, highly suggestive of a pineoblastoma. Prompt neurosurgical consultation and CSF staging are recommended.

MRI and MR venography (MRV) demonstrate an absence of the normal flow void within the posterior aspect of the superior sagittal sinus and right transverse sinus, replaced by hyperintense clot on T1/T2. Associated subcortical venous congestion and cortical edema are present in the right parietal lobe.

Impression: Dural venous sinus thrombosis involving the posterior superior sagittal and right transverse sinuses. Non-hemorrhagic venous congestion is noted in the adjacent parietal lobe.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. The anterior callosal body and rostrum are present, but the posterior body and splenium are absent. This is associated with mild colpocephaly, with the occipital horns measuring 11.2 mm on the left and 10.9 mm on the right. Cortical sulcal development is otherwise appropriate for the gestational age.

The brainstem and cerebellum are intact. Impression: Partial corpus callosum agenesis with associated mild colpocephaly. High-resolution postnatal imaging is recommended.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates marked dilation and dysfunction of the right ventricle, with an end-diastolic volume index of 122 mL/m2 and an ejection fraction of 34%. Regional wall motion abnormalities are present, including dyskinesis and micro-aneurysms within the right ventricular outflow tract and inferior wall (triangle of dysplasia). Bright-blood and late gadolinium enhancement sequences reveal areas of fatty infiltration and focal fibrosis within the right ventricular free wall. The left ventricle is normal in size and function (EF 58%).

Impression: Findings are highly characteristic of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), meeting major Task Force criteria based on right ventricular volume, function, and regional wall motion abnormalities.

Brain MRI reveals a large cystic mass in the right cerebellar hemisphere, measuring 3.8 x 3.2 x 3.5 cm. The lesion features a prominent, intensely enhancing mural nodule along its posterolateral aspect. Mass effect is demonstrated upon the fourth ventricle, which is compressed and displaced to the left, resulting in mild upstream dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles. There is no surrounding vasogenic edema or restricted diffusion.

Impression: Highly characteristic appearance of a juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Associated mild obstructive hydrocephalus is present, and neurosurgical evaluation is recommended.

MRI of the brain demonstrates a well-circumscribed CSF-density extra-axial cystic lesion located in the left middle cranial fossa, measuring 3.8 x 2.2 x 2.5 cm. The cyst follows CSF signal intensity on all sequences, including complete suppression on FLAIR and absence of restricted diffusion on DWI. There is mild scalloping of the adjacent squamous portion of the temporal bone and minimal mass effect on the adjacent temporal lobe.

Impression: Left middle cranial fossa arachnoid cyst (Galassi Type II) with minimal mass effect and no associated hydrocephalus. Suggest clinical monitoring.

Fetal MRI evaluated at 21 weeks gestation demonstrates findings consistent with bilateral renal agenesis and Potter's sequence. There is severe oligohydramnios present, limiting the resolution of some structures. Neither kidney can be identified in the renal fossae or within the pelvis. The fetal urinary bladder is non-distended and cannot be visualized. Fetal lungs appear globally small, compressed by the severe oligohydramnios.

The intracranial structures are grossly intact, but limited by positioning; the ventricular atrium is normal at 5.2 mm. Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis associated with severe oligohydramnios and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia, consistent with Potter's sequence.

Brain MRI demonstrates prominent leptomeningeal enhancement over the left cerebral hemisphere, particularly in the temporo-parieto-occipital region. There is associated progressive atrophy of the left cerebral hemisphere with overlying calvarial thickening and enlargement of the left choroid plexus. Cortical calcifications are suggested on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) in a gyriform pattern.

Impression: Neuroimaging findings characteristic of unilateral Sturge-Weber syndrome involving the left hemisphere. Mild progressive cerebral atrophy noted.

Fetal MRI at 23 weeks gestation demonstrates complete non-visualization of both fetal kidneys. The renal fossae are empty, and there is a classic 'lying down' sign of the adrenal glands, which are elongated and parallel to the spine. Extremely severe oligohydramnios (virtually anhydramnios) is present, severely limiting image resolution of peripheral fetal limbs, though the core anatomy remains visible. The lungs are severely compressed and hypoplastic.

Brain structures are intact, though evaluation is limited. Ventricles are within normal limits. Impression: Bilateral renal agenesis associated with anhydramnios and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia. This is a highly critical finding with a very poor prognosis.

MR examination of the brain demonstrates normal anatomical alignment and normal signal characteristics of the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, and brainstem. There is no evidence of demyelinating disease, acute ischemia, or mass lesions. The intracranial arterial flow voids are intact, and the venous drainage is normal. Orbits and paranasal sinuses are unremarkable.

Impression: Normal MR imaging of the brain. No intracranial structural abnormalities or acute pathology identified.

Fetal MRI performed at 24 weeks gestation shows normal intracranial and extracranial development. The cerebral hemispheres demonstrate appropriate, age-specific sulcation with early formation of the parieto-occipital and cingulate sulci. The ventricular system is symmetric and normal in caliber, with the lateral ventricular atrium measuring 5.8 mm. The corpus callosum, cerebellum, and brainstem are structurally intact and appropriate for gestational age.

The fetal chest, abdomen, and musculoskeletal systems are unremarkable. Amniotic fluid volume is subjectively normal. Impression: Completely normal fetal MRI study demonstrating age-appropriate brain development and normal anatomy at 24 weeks gestation.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is performed to evaluate atypical pediatric chest discomfort. Multiplanar, multisequence cine and anatomical imaging demonstrate normal cardiac chamber dimensions, myocardial mass, and global systolic function. The left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 63% and the right ventricular ejection fraction at 60%. No regional wall motion abnormalities are identified. No late gadolinium enhancement is observed to suggest myocardial scar or fibrosis.

Great vessels and coronary artery origins appear normal, with a left-sided aortic arch. Impression: Unremarkable pediatric cardiac MRI with normal biventricular volumes and function. No structural abnormalities, shunts, or perfusion anomalies are demonstrated.

Fetal MRI at 35 weeks gestation demonstrates proximal shortening of all long limbs (rhizomelia) and mild frontal bossing of the skull, highly consistent with achondroplasia. Fetal hand evaluation reveals a trident configuration of the fingers. The fetal brain shows normal intracranial anatomy, with lateral ventricles measuring 7.5 mm. Sulcation and gyral maturation are advanced and appropriate for 35 weeks gestation.

Impression: Skeletal dysplasia findings at 35 weeks gestation, highly characteristic of fetal achondroplasia. Normal fetal brain structures and development.

Cardiac MR imaging demonstrates normal cardiac morphology and ventricular function. The left ventricular end-diastolic volume is 72 mL/m2 with an ejection fraction of 62%. The right ventricular end-diastolic volume is 75 mL/m2 with an ejection fraction of 60%. There is no evidence of valvular dysfunction, congenital malformations, or anomalous pulmonary venous return. T1 and T2 mapping values are within normal limits, and there is no late gadolinium enhancement.

Impression: Normal cardiac MRI study. There is no evidence of structural, functional, or inflammatory cardiac pathology.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates a large, circumferential pericardial effusion measuring up to 2.1 cm in the posterior and lateral gutters. The pericardium itself is thickened and demonstrates intense late gadolinium enhancement, suggestive of active inflammation. Real-time cine sequences show no evidence of diastolic right ventricular collapse, although there is mild respiratory variation of trans-mitral inflow.

Impression: Acute pericarditis with a moderate-to-large circumferential pericardial effusion. No definitive cardiac tamponade physiology is seen on the current scan, but clinical monitoring is advised.

Fetal MRI performed at 27 weeks gestation demonstrates normal development. Brain maturation, including operculization of the sylvian fissures, is normal. Both lateral ventricles are completely normal in size, measuring 5.7 mm and 5.8 mm. The brainstem, cerebellum, and spine are fully formed and show no congenital defects. Amniotic fluid volume is within normal limits.

Impression: Normal fetal MRI study at 27 weeks gestation. Cortical sulcation and ventricular metrics are entirely normal for age.

Fetal MRI at 25 weeks gestation reveals features highly suggestive of a skeletal dysplasia. There is profound shortening of all visualized long bones (severe micromelia) with bowing of the femurs. The fetal thorax is extremely narrow and bell-shaped, with short ribs. Skull mineralization is preserved, but macrocephaly with frontal bossing is present. Brain parenchyma and ventricles (atrium 7.0 mm) are within normal parameters.

Impression: Fetal skeletal dysplasia with severe micromelia and a narrow, hypoplastic thorax at 25 weeks gestation, concerning for thanatophoric dysplasia.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal internal cardiac structures, ventricular volumes, and wall thicknesses. There is no evidence of intracardiac shunt, valvular stenosis, or regurgitation. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 63%, and right ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. No focal wall motion abnormalities are identified. Myocardial T1/T2 mapping values and late gadolinium enhancement sequences are normal.

Impression: Normal pediatric cardiac MRI. No cardiac morphology, perfusion, or functional abnormalities are demonstrated.

Fetal MRI at 32 weeks gestation reveals normal fetal development. The cerebral cortex shows well-advanced sulcation patterns, including clearly defined central, precentral, and postcentral sulci, entirely appropriate for 32 weeks. The lateral ventricles are normal, with the atrium measuring 6.1 mm on the left and 5.9 mm on the right. The corpus callosum and brainstem are intact.

Fetal chest, abdomen, and skeletal structures are normal, showing expected fetal anatomy. No masses or organomegaly are identified. Impression: Unremarkable fetal MRI at 32 weeks gestation with normal, age-appropriate intracranial and extracranial development.

Cardiac MRI shows Ebstein's anomaly. There is marked apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve by 22 mm relative to the mitral valve plane. This results in severe 'atrialization' of the inlet portion of the right ventricle. The functional right ventricle is small and demonstrates mild systolic dysfunction (RVEF 44%). There is severe tricuspid regurgitation with massive dilation of the right atrium.

Impression: Severe Ebstein's anomaly with significant tricuspid valve displacement, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and severe right atrial dilation.

Cardiac MRI was performed on a 5-year-old male with an atypical heart murmur detected during routine screening. Multiplanar steady-state free precession (SSFP) cine sequences show normal cardiac chamber dimensions and wall thickness. There is no evidence of atrial or ventricular septal defects, abnormal valvular structure, or vascular anomalies. Global and regional biventricular systolic functions are completely normal, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 64% and a right ventricular ejection fraction of 60%.

Impression: Unremarkable pediatric cardiac MRI with no structural defects, chamber dilation, or ventricular dysfunction identified. The murmur is likely physiologic (innocent) in nature.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation demonstrates complete absence of the corpus callosum. There is characteristic colpocephaly with dilated occipital horns measuring 12.5 mm and 12.1 mm, and a parallel configuration of the lateral ventricles (steer-horn appearance on coronal views). The third ventricle is superiorly displaced and dilated. Cortical sulcation demonstrates atypical, radially oriented gyri pointing toward the third ventricle, typical of callosal agenesis.

The cerebello-pontine angle and cerebellar vermis appear normal. No other associated midline structural defects are visualized. Impression: Complete agenesis of the corpus callosum with secondary colpocephaly.

Fetal MRI at 22 weeks gestation demonstrates normal anatomy. The cerebral hemispheres exhibit appropriate primary sulcation for the gestational age. The ventricular system is within normal limits, with the atrium measuring 5.5 mm bilaterally. The brainstem, cerebellum, and corpus callosum are fully intact and well-developed. The thorax, abdominal viscera, and spine are unremarkable.

Impression: Completely normal fetal MRI study demonstrating age-appropriate structural and central nervous system development at 22 weeks gestation.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates Ebstein's anomaly of the tricuspid valve. There is severe apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve by 22 mm, resulting in marked atrialization of the right ventricle. The functional right ventricle is severely small and dyskinetic. Massive tricuspid regurgitation is observed, filling the giant right atrium. The left ventricular morphology and function are preserved (EF 59%).

Impression: Classic Ebstein's anomaly with severe tricuspid valve apical displacement, massive tricuspid regurgitation, and a severely dilated, atrialized right ventricle.

Brain MRI demonstrates a lobulated, complex cystic and solid mass centered within the suprasellar region measuring 3.2 x 2.8 x 2.5 cm. The solid components show patchy peripheral enhancement, and small intrinsic T1 hyperintensities consistent with proteinaceous/cholesterol-rich fluid are present. The mass exerts significant superior pressure, displacing and flattening the optic chiasm and elevating the floor of the third ventricle.

Impression: Suprasellar cystic-solid mass, highly suggestive of an adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma. Significant compression of the visual pathways is noted; urgent ophthalmologic and endocrine evaluation recommended.

MRI of the brain demonstrates an ill-defined, non-enhancing area of T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the left temporal lobe, extending into the insular cortex. The lesion measures approximately 4.5 x 3.8 cm and exerts mild mass effect, manifesting as partial effacement of the overlying cortical sulci and the left temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. No areas of restricted diffusion or abnormal contrast enhancement are seen.

Impression: Infiltrating T2/FLAIR-hyperintense mass in the left temporal lobe without enhancement, highly suspicious for a low-grade glioma (such as a diffuse astrocytoma). MR spectroscopy is recommended for further characterization.

MRI of the brain demonstrates a suprasellar, heterogenous mass measuring approximately 3.1 x 2.7 x 2.6 cm. The mass contains both solid enhancing elements and hyperintense cystic components, with peripheral calcifications noted on gradient recall echo (GRE) sequences. The pituitary stalk is compressed and displaced posteriorly, and there is mild compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are within normal limits with no hydrocephalus.

Impression: Sellar/suprasellar mass with solid, cystic, and calcified components, most consistent with an adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma. Optic chiasm compression noted; endocrine and ophthalmology consultations are indicated.

MRI of the neonatal brain shows moderate hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis with a keyhole-shaped communication between the fourth ventricle and the enlarged cisterna magna. The posterior fossa is moderately expanded. The cerebral hemispheres demonstrate normal myelination patterns for a two-month-old infant, with no signs of intracranial hemorrhage or focal ischemic injury.

Impression: Dandy-Walker variant characterized by cerebellar vermian hypoplasia and moderate posterior fossa expansion. Clinical correlation with pediatric neurology is advised.

Brain MRI reveals multifocal, asymmetric, poorly-demarcated hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR sequences scattered throughout the subcortical and deep white matter of both cerebral hemispheres. Several of these lesions demonstrate faint, incomplete ring-like enhancement after gadolinium administration. No significant mass effect, midline shift, or large territorial ischemic injury is identified.

Impression: Multifocal white matter lesions, most consistent with Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) given the presentation. Clinical and imaging follow-up is recommended to differentiate from pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis.

Fetal MRI at 29 weeks gestation demonstrates severe rhizomelic shortening of all long bones, consistent with a skeletal dysplasia such as thanatophoric dysplasia. The femurs are abnormally curved, resembling a "telephone receiver" configuration. Mild platyspondyly of the thoracic and lumbar spine is visualized. Fetal brain evaluation demonstrates a normal ventricular system (atrial width 7.2 mm) and expected sulcation patterns for 29 weeks gestation, including clear parieto-occipital sulci.

Impression: Skeletal dysplasia at 29 weeks gestation, highly suspicious for thanatophoric dysplasia given severe rhizomelic limb shortening and femoral curvature.

MRI of the heart demonstrates normal cardiac anatomy and great vessel connections. Right and left ventricular dimensions, volumes, and wall thicknesses are entirely within the normal reference ranges for the patient's body surface area. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 64% and right ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. Valvular leaflets are thin and mobile with no hemodynamically significant stenosis or regurgitation. No late gadolinium enhancement is identified.

Impression: Unremarkable and completely normal pediatric cardiac MRI. No congenital anomalies or myocardial diseases demonstrated.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a 7-year-old female with a family history of congenital heart defects. Multiplanar cine MRI shows normal biventricular volumes and preserved contractility, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 63% and right ventricular ejection fraction of 61%. No atrial or ventricular septal defects are visualized. Great vessel and coronary anatomy are normal.

No late gadolinium enhancement or abnormal myocardial signal is detected. Impression: Completely normal pediatric cardiac MRI. No congenital anomalies or cardiomyopathy identified.

Fetal MRI at 24 weeks gestation reveals a right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The liver is herniated into the right thoracic cavity, causing a significant mediastinal shift to the left. The right lung is severely compressed and virtually unidentifiable, and the left lung is moderately compressed. Intracranial anatomy is unremarkable, with symmetric lateral ventricles measuring 5.4 mm at the atrium and normal 24-week sulcation.

No other anomalies are identified in the spine or abdomen. Impression: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver herniation ('liver-up'), resulting in severe mediastinal shift and severe pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal MRI at 26 weeks gestation reveals a right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Part of the right hepatic lobe, the gallbladder, and some small bowel loops have herniated into the right posterior thoracic cavity. There is severe leftward mediastinal shift with compression of the heart and severe compression of both lungs. The fetal brain structures show expected development, with normal ventricular caliber (atrial width 6.2 mm) and normal sulcation for 26 weeks.

Impression: Right-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia with liver herniation and severe pulmonary hypoplasia. High-risk perinatal management and multidisciplinary planning advised.

Cardiac MRI of a 3-month-old female reveals an anomalous origin of the left main coronary artery arising from the posterior aspect of the main pulmonary artery. The right coronary artery is significantly dilated and tortuous, measuring 3.5 mm at its origin, supplying collateral vessels to the left coronary system. Retrograde flow from the left coronary artery into the pulmonary artery is visualized. The left ventricle is moderately dilated with global hypokinesia, and the left ventricular ejection fraction is reduced at 35%. Prominent subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is observed in the anterolateral wall and papillary muscles, representing subendocardial infarction.

Impression: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) associated with left ventricular dilation, moderately severe systolic dysfunction (LVEF 35%), and anterolateral subendocardial myocardial infarction.

Fetal MRI at 27 weeks gestation demonstrates severe shortening of all long bones, with the femora showing a characteristic curved 'telephone receiver' morphology, highly suggestive of thanatophoric dysplasia. The chest is extremely narrow and bell-shaped, with severely restricted lung volumes. There is prominent macrocephaly and a cloverleaf skull deformity is noted with frontal bossing.

Intracranial structures demonstrate mild temporal lobe ventriculomegaly with an atrial width of 10.2 mm and deep, abnormal temporal sulcation. Impression: Severe skeletal dysplasia with features highly characteristic of Thanatophoric Dysplasia Type I, including severe micromelia, narrow chest cavity, and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia.

Cardiac MRI reveals prominent hypertrabeculation and deep intertrabecular recesses within the apical and mid-lateral segments of the left ventricle. The ratio of non-compacted to compacted myocardium at end-diastole is measured at 2.4:1, meeting diagnostic criteria for non-compaction. Left ventricular systolic function is mildly depressed with an ejection fraction of 49%.

No focal late gadolinium enhancement is observed. Right ventricular size and function are unremarkable. Impression: Left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) with mild global left ventricular systolic dysfunction, without evidence of myocardial fibrosis.

Fetal MRI at 31 weeks gestation reveals entirely normal and age-appropriate anatomy. The fetal brain demonstrates normal primary and secondary sulcation, including progressive operculization of the Sylvian fissure. The bilateral lateral ventricles are completely symmetric, with the atria measuring 6.5 mm. The midline structures, including the corpus callosum and septum pellucidum, are normal in appearance.

Fetal thoracic and abdominal viscera are structurally normal. The kidneys and bladder are normal in size and signal intensity, and amniotic fluid volume is physiologic. Impression: Normal fetal MRI study demonstrating appropriate development for 31 weeks gestation.

Fetal MRI at 36 weeks gestation shows excellent development of the brain parenchyma. The sulcation and gyral patterns are highly complex, with well-formed secondary and tertiary sulci appropriate for late third-trimester gestation. The lateral ventricular atria measure 5.2 mm and 5.5 mm. The brainstem, cerebellum, and corpus callosum are fully formed and normal in appearance. 

No chest, abdominal wall, or extremity defects are identified. The amniotic fluid index is normal. Impression: Completely normal, late third-trimester fetal MRI demonstrating appropriate neurological and structural maturation.

Fetal MRI at 21 weeks gestation demonstrates a severely distended urinary bladder with a thickened wall and a dilated proximal posterior urethra, exhibiting the classic 'keyhole' sign. There is severe bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, with the renal pelves measuring 12 mm on the left and 14 mm on the right, accompanied by thinning of the renal parenchyma. Moderate-to-severe oligohydramnios is present, which restricts thoracic growth and causes mild pulmonary hypoplasia. The fetal brain appears normal, with symmetric lateral ventricles (atrial width 5.4 mm).

Impression: Severe bladder outlet obstruction, highly indicative of posterior urethral valves (PUV). Associated with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, renal parenchymal thinning, and oligohydramnios. High risk of pulmonary hypoplasia.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates normal, age-appropriate intracranial structures. The operculization of the sylvian fissure and early temporal sulcation are completely normal. The lateral ventricular atrium measures 6.0 mm bilaterally, indicating no ventriculomegaly. The brainstem, cerebellar vermis, and corpus callosum are fully visualized and intact.

Fetal body, thorax, and abdominal anatomy are unremarkable. Impression: Completely normal fetal MRI study demonstrating appropriate structural brain and somatic development for 28 weeks.

MR examination of the brain demonstrates multiple discrete, ovoid, T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions within the periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial white matter. Several of these lesions are oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles, consistent with Dawson's fingers. Following contrast administration, two active lesions in the left frontal lobe demonstrate incomplete ring enhancement, indicating active demyelination.

Impression: Multi-focal demyelinating disease, highly suggestive of pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis, demonstrating dissemination in space and time. Recommend correlation with cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands.

Cardiac MRI shows thickened mitral valve leaflets, particularly the anterior leaflet, with restricted diastolic excursion. Multi-slice phase-contrast flow assessment reveals severe mitral regurgitation with a calculated regurgitant fraction of 41%. The left atrium is severely dilated with a volume index of 64 ml/m², and the left ventricle is mildly dilated with a normal ejection fraction (59%).

Impression: Chronic rheumatic heart disease showing severe mitral regurgitation with associated moderate left atrial dilation. Left ventricular systolic function remains preserved.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates normal cardiac architecture. Both left and right ventricles show normal end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes for body surface area. Left ventricular ejection fraction is calculated at 65%, and right ventricular ejection fraction is 61%. No valvular regurgitation, stenosis, or intracardiac shunts are visualized. Late gadolinium enhancement images show no areas of pathological myocardial enhancement.

Impression: Unremarkable cardiac MRI. Normal biventricular volumes and systolic function with no evidence of structural heart disease or myocardial fibrosis.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC). There is a pronounced two-layered myocardium within the left ventricular apex and lateral wall, with a non-compacted to compacted myocardial thickness ratio of 2.6 during end-diastole. Deep intertrabecular recesses are visualized communicating with the LV cavity. The left ventricle is mildly dilated with mild global systolic dysfunction (LVEF 48%).

Impression: Left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) with mild left ventricular enlargement and mild systolic dysfunction.

Pediatric cardiac MRI demonstrates findings characteristic of Ebstein's anomaly. There is marked apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve, resulting in 'atrialization' of the inlet portion of the right ventricle. The functional right ventricle is small and demonstrates reduced systolic function (RVEF 34%). Severe, free tricuspid regurgitation is noted on velocity-encoded sequences.

Impression: Ebstein's anomaly with severe tricuspid regurgitation and moderate right ventricular dysfunction. Left ventricular size and function are preserved.

Brain MRI shows no acute or chronic intra-axial abnormalities. The ventricular system, basal cisterns, and subarachnoid spaces are normal. Flow voids in the major circle of Willis vessels are preserved. Visualized portions of the orbits and skull base are unremarkable.

Impression: Unremarkable MR imaging of the brain. Normal study with no diagnostic etiology for syncopal episodes or localized neurology.

Fetal MRI at 22 weeks gestation demonstrates a large occipital encephalocele. A midline defect in the posterior occipital bone measures approximately 1.4 cm. Through this defect, a herniation sac containing meninges and a small portion of dysplastic cerebellar tissue is visualized. This is associated with mild downward traction on the midbrain and ventriculomegaly (atrial width 11.8 mm).

Impression: Midline fetal occipital encephalocele containing dysplastic neural elements. Associated mild ventriculomegaly is noted.

Brain MRI evaluated a 10-year-old child with persistent post-traumatic cephalalgia following a minor fall. Multiplanar, multisequence brain imaging shows completely normal appearance of the cerebral cortex, subcortical white matter, and deep gray nuclei. There is no evidence of intracranial bleed, skull fracture, extra-axial fluid collections, or parenchymal contusion. The ventricles and basilar cisterns are normal.

Impression: Normal brain MRI with no acute traumatic or chronic structural abnormalities. No intracranial correlates identified to explain the patient's persistent post-traumatic headaches.

Fetal MRI at 28 weeks gestation demonstrates significant bilateral ventriculomegaly. The left lateral ventricle atrium measures 14.5 mm and the right measures 13.8 mm, indicating moderate-to-severe ventriculomegaly. There is associated thinning of the corpus callosum. The cerebral sulcation and gyration pattern appears slightly delayed for 28 weeks gestation, with shallow sulcation noted in the frontoparietal lobes. The third ventricle is mildly dilated.

No aqueductal stenosis or extra-axial fluid collections are clearly visualized. Impression: Moderate-to-severe bilateral fetal ventriculomegaly at 28 weeks gestation. Recommend prenatal tracking and postnatal pediatric neurosurgical consultation.

Cardiac MRI evaluates a patient with transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) status post-arterial switch operation. The anatomical left ventricle supports the systemic circulation and shows normal size and function (LVEF 59%). There is mild dilation of the neo-aortic root measuring 3.6 cm. No significant narrowing is identified at the coronary reimplantation sites. The branch pulmonary arteries demonstrate normal flow without significant stenosis.

Impression: Post-arterial switch operation for d-TGA showing preserved systemic LV function and mild dilation of the neo-aortic root without other post-operative complications.

Neonatal brain MRI demonstrates multiple areas of subependymal calcification along the walls of the lateral ventricles, best seen as signal loss on T2* GRE imaging. Bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria is noted with a thickened cortical ribbon and multiple small, poorly defined gyri. Dilated ventricles and ventriculomegaly are present with prominent extra-axial CSF spaces.

Impression: Severe congenital brain malformations including perisylvian polymicrogyria and subependymal calcifications, highly indicative of in utero infection such as congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV).

MR examination of the brain reveals multiple subependymal nodules lining the lateral ventricles, some showing low signal on T2 and high signal on T1. Additionally, there are several wedge-shaped cortical and subcortical tubers demonstrating T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, predominantly in the frontal and parietal lobes. No evidence of subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) is noted at the foramina of Monro.

Impression: Brain MRI findings are highly characteristic of tuberous sclerosis complex, demonstrating subependymal nodules and multiple cortical/subcortical tubers. No hydrocephalus or SEGA identified.

Brain MRI was obtained following a first-time unprovoked seizure. The cerebral hemispheres demonstrate normal myelination patterns appropriate for age. No focal cortical thickening, dysplasia, or hippocampal asymmetry is identified. The ventricular system, corpus callosum, and posterior fossa structures are normal in size and morphological structure.
